title: Is It Really a Monster?
sub: Grades 3–4 · Pareidolia · How your brain fills in the dark
objective: Students will learn that the brain is a pattern-seeking machine that sees faces and threats where none exist, which poster 1 calls **pareidolia**. They will find faces in everyday objects, explain why a brain built to spot danger would rather raise 100 fake alarms than miss one real predator, and use that knowledge to check what is really there when the dark plays tricks.

objectives.heading: By the end of this lesson you will be able to:
objectives.why: Shapes in the dark can feel like monsters. Knowing why your brain makes them helps you check what is really there.

items.text: explain that your brain is a pattern-seeking machine that sees faces and threats where none exist: pareidolia
items.question: explain what pareidolia is?

items.text: find a face in an everyday object, and say what your brain is doing
items.question: find a face that isn’t there, and say why you see it?

items.text: explain why a brain would rather see 100 fake threats than miss one real predator

items.question: talk back to your brain when it imagines the worst?

materials: Poster 1 or the *Show your class* page (page 3), projected
A flashlight, if you have one, for a shadow on the wall
questions: Where have you seen a face in something that wasn’t a face?
Why might it be safer to see a fake threat than to miss a real one?
What does the clawed hand make you imagine? What is it really?
What could you say to yourself when your brain imagines the worst?
questionsLabel: Questions to ask in front of the poster
connection: **Visit the exhibition:** on poster 1, find *Pareidolia: Seeing Monsters Everywhere*, then the spider and the clawed hand. Ask: *what shapes did the designer use to make you feel scared?*
**Online:** in *What Scares You?*, the Rustling Bushes counts fake alarms and missed tigers.

steps.title: Faces everywhere
script: Ask: *“Look around the room. Can you find a face that isn’t really a face?”* Give students a minute to look. They might find two screws and a handle, a wall socket, a clock, the front of a car in the parking lot. Ask each to point out the *eyes* and the *mouth*. Then: *“Nobody drew a face there. So who made it a face?”*

screen.question: Look around the room. Can you find a face that isn’t really a face?

steps.purpose: Discover pareidolia before naming it: everyone finds faces that aren’t there.
students: Find one in the room. Point to its eyes and mouth.

steps.title: A pattern-seeking machine
script: Read the poster: *“Your brain is a pattern-seeking machine that sees faces and threats where none exist.”* The poster calls this **pareidolia**. Your brain is so good at finding faces that it finds them in sockets, clouds and cars.

screen.text: Your brain is a pattern-seeking machine that sees faces and threats where none exist.

steps.purpose: Name what students just did: pareidolia.
students: Where else have you seen a face that wasn’t there?

steps.title: Shapes in the dark
script: In the dark there is less to see, so the brain fills in more. The poster says shadow people are *just your brain turning random darkness into human shapes.* Show the poster’s clawed hand: a flat cream shape. Your brain does the rest. If you have a flashlight, make a shadow on the wall with your hand, and ask what students see.

screen.alt: The poster’s clawed hand: a flat cream shape with long, curved fingers
screen.caption: Shadow people? Just your brain turning random darkness into human shapes.

steps.purpose: See how a plain shape becomes a monster when the brain fills it in.
students: What does your brain say this is?

steps.title: Better safe than sorry
script: Why would a brain work like this? *“This isn’t a flaw—it’s by design. Our brains know it is better to see 100 fake threats than miss one real predator.”* Long ago, those who assumed rustling bushes held tigers lived longer. The poster calls this **negativity bias**: when it isn’t sure, your brain imagines disasters, because it is trying to keep you safe.

screen.text: This isn’t a flaw—it’s by design. Our brains know it is better to see 100 fake threats than miss one real predator.
screen.cite: Poster 1 · The Science of Being Scared

steps.purpose: Understand why the brain is built to raise fake alarms.
students: Which costs more: a fake alarm, or missing a real predator?

steps.title: Choose a handout
script: Students choose a handout. All three hunt for faces that aren’t there and explain why the brain raises fake alarms.

levels.name: Green Level
levels.summary: Circle the eyes and mouth in three everyday objects, turn three shapes into faces, match the new words to their meanings, and finish sentences about why the brain sees faces.

levels.name: Yellow Level
levels.summary: Record three faces found in the classroom, explain the poster’s sentence in their own words, decide whether a fake alarm or a missed predator costs more, and explain shadow people.

levels.name: Red Level
levels.summary: Ask questions about the poster’s experiment on imaginary faces, weigh the costs of two kinds of mistake, design a face test for the class, and write advice for a younger child afraid of the dark.

steps.purpose: Practice spotting and explaining pareidolia at the right level of challenge.
students: Choose Green, Yellow or Red. All three hunt for faces and explain the brain’s fake alarms.

steps.title: Talk back to your brain
script: Ask the poster’s own question: *“When has your brain imagined the worst? What could you say to yourself when it does?”* Pairs share; collect a few lines on the board, such as *it’s just my brain filling in the dark* or *let me look again.*

screen.question: When has your brain imagined the worst? What could you say to yourself when it does?

steps.purpose: Turn what students know about the brain into something they can say to themselves.
students: Share one thing you could say.

steps.title: Look back
script: Then ask the objectives back, from the screen or page 1: *“Can you now…?”* Students show a thumb up, sideways or down. Exit question: *“What is pareidolia, and why does your brain do it?”*
